finding: Rule 1 ("Every assertion must fail on today's tree") is unsatisfiable for most of this release's tasks, and §12 states no exemption. Non-Goal 1 requires §6, §7 and §8.1 to be behaviour-neutral, so an assertion accompanying an inline (§6.2), a dead-branch removal (§6.3), a redundant-assertion removal (§7.2) or a doc de-duplication (§8.1) passes before and after by construction. §2.1 makes the conflict explicit for tests: the required evidence is "the surviving test that fails when the original defect is reintroduced" — a test that passes on today's tree is exactly what that row demands. Read literally, rule 1 forbids the evidence §2.1 mandates; read charitably, it is silent about which tasks it governs, and two engineers writing acceptance for a §7.2 removal will disagree on whether the task is admissible at all.

resolved.evidence: Rule 1 is scoped to assertions accompanying a behaviour change, and section 12 now names which sections are outcome sections and which apply a judgement whose acceptance shape is section 2.1's removal contract.

suggestion: Scope rule 1 to the behaviour-changing sections (§3, §4, §5, §9.1, §9.2, §9.3) plus the new guard/equality tests of §5, §8.2 and §8.3, and state the complementary rule for the behaviour-neutral sweeps: the named surviving assertion must pass before and after, and the gate is what proves the sweep changed nothing.

finding: Two recorded high fixes died in this round's deletion. Round 2 idx (mask-regenerated-by-generator) was resolved with "The generator is addressed in the same paragraph: later releases omit --quality-gate at init", and round 3 (generator-recipe-not-updated) was resolved with "the --quality-gate flag comes out of CLAUDE.md and skills/tp/SKILL.md, which is what stops the next init from re-creating the override." Round 5 deleted that entire paragraph and replaced it with an outcome scoped to "this release's task file". Verified against the current tree, not the evidence line: CLAUDE.md:190 still reads `tp init spec/<version>.md --quality-gate "go test ./... && golangci-lint run"`, and skills/tp/SKILL.md still carries the flag at lines 32, 58 and the literal pre-race gate string at line 48. The current §5's only documentation mandate is that SKILL.md "recommends -race" — it does not touch CLAUDE.md at all, and CLAUDE.md is the document v0.35.0's unattended run follows for step 3. So the next init-authored task file re-creates a task-level quality_gate masking the project gate, the unattended run this release is explicitly scheduled to protect executes every close without -race, and the guard — now bounded to "this release's task file" — cannot see it. A corroborating tell that the deletion was not propagated: §8.3 still says "Note the interaction with §5 — a flag stays in the inventory even when the documented workflow stops recommending it", a note written against a §5 clause that no longer exists.

resolved.evidence: The doc-recipe edit is restored as a constraint in section 5: CLAUDE.md and skills/tp/SKILL.md drop the --quality-gate flag, without which the next init re-creates the override.

suggestion: Restore the generator half of §5 as an outcome rather than a route: the documented init recipe in CLAUDE.md and skills/tp/SKILL.md must not instruct a gate string without -race, so a task file authored by a later release does not silently mask the project gate. Leave which lines change to decomposition, but state the requirement, and either restore §5's flag-recommendation clause or drop §8.3's now-dangling reference to it.

finding: Four recorded fixes at §8.2 (unbound-equality-source high; undefined-oracle, undefined-set-boundary, internal-count-mismatch medium) all rested on one construction — "the engine gains an exported enumeration of its lint rule identifiers and emits rule identifiers from it" plus item 9's binding assertion. Round 4 correctly disproved that construction (enumeration-scope-mismatch, high: lint.go emits acceptance-quality and affected-files-scope, so an engine enumeration holds 14 while tp emits 16), and round 5 removed it. But the replacement — "Sourcing each side is decomposition's problem" — reopens all four, and the prior rounds have already measured that no honest source exists inside this release's Non-Goals: construction by typing is excluded by Non-Goal 7 (§8.2 says so itself); an engine enumeration undercounts by two, measured; and collecting the emitted side by observation undercounts badly, since the round-2 text recorded that only 7 distinct rules fire across all of this repository's specs. What is left is a hand-written list on each side, which drifts identically and passes the equality — the exact drift §8.2 exists to prevent. Unlike §5 and §12, where delegation hands decomposition a question code can settle, here the review has already established by measurement that the question has no answer within the release's own fences.

resolved.evidence: Section 8.2 no longer hands the sourcing problem down unqualified. It records what review measured as impossible and asks for what remains achievable: a collected list checked against the table, with the collection's blind spot recorded beside it.

suggestion: Either name the one honestly-collectible source for the emitted side (for example: the union over both emitting packages, with the requirement that a new emitting package fails the test rather than being silently missed), or accept that the emitted side cannot be sourced within Non-Goal 7 and narrow §8.2's outcome to what is achievable — e.g. the table is brought complete once against a measured set, and the checked equality is deferred to the version that may refactor emission.

finding: §10.2's entire deliverable is "The recipe is documented in the reference, not in `skills/tp/SKILL.md`", and the reference is the one row of §8.1's table identified by a role rather than a path — `README.md`, `skills/tp/SKILL.md` and `CLAUDE.md` are named as files, "Reference" is not. §10.2 is documentation-only, so the target file is the whole acceptance: two engineers can satisfy it in two different files and neither is wrong by the text. Unlike §8.2 and §8.3, no equality test would catch the divergence, and §8.1's own de-duplication pass cannot decide whether a fact is duplicated when one of its four homes is unnamed.
suggestion: Put the path in §8.1's table row (as the other three rows do); §10.2 then inherits an unambiguous target and §8.1's ownership rule becomes checkable against four named files.

finding: Rule 1 prescribes a procedure ("Verify by running it before the fix, not after") but names no artifact that records it, so nothing distinguishes an assertion that was verified failing from one whose author asserts it was. Every other verification obligation in this spec lands somewhere checkable: §2.1 puts the removal justification in the closing evidence, §6.1 puts clone dispositions at the site, §7.1 puts the guard list in a committed file. Rule 1 alone produces no residue, which makes it the one rule in §12 that a reviewer cannot audit after the fact — the same failure mode §7 exists to fix (a guard nobody re-derived).
suggestion: Give rule 1 the residue §2.1 already models: the closing evidence carries one line per new assertion naming the assertion and the failure observed against the unfixed tree. It needs no tooling and makes the rule reviewable at task-list review, where §2 already puts the operator.

finding: §12 item 2 ("A test and the change it covers close in the same task. The gate runs at every close, so a split leaves the earlier close red.") is a near-verbatim restatement of an existing CLAUDE.md self-development rule ("A change and the test it invalidates belong to the SAME task (v0.31.2 lesson). The gate runs at every `tp done` ..."). The same spec assigns CLAUDE.md ownership of "this repository's own conventions and its self-development loop" (§8.1 table) and rules that "Anything duplicated across two homes is cut from the non-owner" (§8.1). So the section that survived the round-3/4 deletion re-creates, inside this release, exactly the second home §8 exists to remove — and it is a structured numbered item, so decomposition must also map it to a task's acceptance, paying for it twice.
suggestion: Delete item 2's body and cite the rule instead ("the same-task rule of CLAUDE.md applies"), or drop the item entirely — the CLAUDE.md rule already binds every task in this repo, which is the only place this spec is decomposed. If the rule is judged to need restating for a fresh decomposer, state it once and say which document owns it, so §8.1's contract is not broken by the spec that mandates it.

finding: §12's premise — "Each section above states the outcome that must become observably true" and "the assertion that proves it ... is authored as task acceptance" — holds for §3, §4, §5, §8.2, §8.3 and §9, but not for §6.2, §6.3, §7.2, §7.3 or §8.1. Those sections state judgement criteria (inline unless a second caller can be named; remove branches that cannot execute; keep the test with the best failure message; cut the duplicate from the non-owner), and a behaviour-neutral removal produces no new assertion at all. Rule 1, "Every assertion must fail on today's tree," is therefore vacuous for roughly half the release, and a decomposer instructed to derive acceptance from "the outcome" finds none in those sections. The evidence form for those tasks does exist — §2.1's named-surviving-coverage contract — but §12 never connects to it, which is the one place the deleted test list did carry weight for the sweeps.
suggestion: Split §12's instruction in two: sections that mandate an observable change get an assertion authored as acceptance under rules 1 and 2; sweep sections (§6.2, §6.3, §7.2, §7.3, §8.1) get acceptance shaped as §2.1 evidence — the enumerated removals plus the surviving coverage each one names — with the gate, not a new assertion, as the proof of behaviour-neutrality.

finding: §12's warrant for deleting the test list — "Each section above states the outcome that must become observably true" — does not hold for the sections that make up most of the release's work. §6.2 states a selection criterion ("Each is inlined unless a second caller exists today and can be named"), §6.3 states a category of branch to delete, §7.2 states a keep/delete judgement between tests, §7.3 states a conversion policy, and §8.1 states an ownership principle. None of them names a state that becomes observably true or false; decomposition can derive an assertion from §3, §4, §5, §8.2, §8.3, §9.1, §9.2 and §9.3, and from the rest it can derive only a judgement. The blanket claim invites an author to invent an outcome where the spec deliberately left a judgement, which is the drift §12 says it removed.
suggestion: Split the claim: name the sections that state an observable outcome and say their assertion is authored at decomposition; say plainly of §6.2, §6.3, §7.2, §7.3 and §8.1 that they state criteria applied under the §2 review and carry no assertion, so nobody looks for one.

finding: §12.1 asserts "TestFileErrorsCarryAHint gains cases rather than changing shape." The test has no cases: it is one ast.Inspect walk over every package source with a hard-coded predicate (`code.Name != "ExitFile"` → skip) and one file-level exemption map. Satisfying §9.2 requires editing that predicate to admit ExitValidation and carrying a second exemption set, and satisfying §9.3 requires lint.go to leave the shared map — both are shape changes to the walk, not added cases. As written, §12.1 tells decomposition the guard is untouched by the very change that rewrites it.
suggestion: Replace with what is true against the code: the guard is a single AST enumeration and it is modified in place — its exit-code predicate widens and its exemption sets are re-derived per code — while remaining one test.

finding: §12.1 claims to be the list of "Existing tests this change invalidates" but covers only the bulk readers (§4) and `TestFileErrorsCarryAHint` (§9.2, §9.3). Two enumerated behaviour changes are absent: §9.1 moves unknown commands and unknown subcommands from exit 1 to exit 2, which invalidates every existing assertion on the old code, and §5 rewrites the project `quality_gate` string in `.tp/config.json`, which invalidates any test pinning today's value (§7.4's phrase "the config guard of §5" implies such a guard is in scope). Rule 2 makes the omission expensive rather than cosmetic: an invalidated test nobody anticipated is discovered as a red gate at close, in a task whose acceptance never mentioned it.
suggestion: Add rows for §9.1 and §5, or restate §12.1's scope as "the invalidations known before decomposition" and require the decomposition step to search for assertions on the old exit code and the old gate string, assigning each to the task that changes it.

finding: The recorded fix for weak-assertion-predicate (medium) was "Test item 5 now asserts equality with the exact gate string instead of a contains check", and the fix for self-referential-oracle (high) was "The guard asserts the resolved gate against the literal string, not against the project value". Round 5 kept only the negative half — "the guard must not compare the resolved value against the project value" — and restated the positive requirement as "the gate resolved for this release's task file runs `-race`", explicitly deferring "what the assertion compares against" to decomposition. A contains-style guard (resolved gate contains "-race") satisfies the one retained constraint in full while passing against a gate weakened to `go test -race ./...` with golangci-lint dropped. That is the same class of predicate the round-1 finding invoked the v0.31.1 lesson against, and it is now reachable again: the section's surviving constraint blocks the self-referential form but not the weak form, and the section's own headline wording ("runs -race") points a decomposer straight at it.
suggestion: Keep the delegation but carry both policy constraints, not one: the guard must compare against a value that does not move when the project gate moves, and it must fail on a gate that drops any component of the gate command, not only on one missing -race.

finding: §6.1 correctly reasons that enabling `dupl` and cleaning the tree must be one task because `.golangci.yml` runs at every close — but stops there. The consequence is that every task closing after that one is also gated by `dupl`, including §7.2/§7.3's test rewrites and §8's new tests. §8.3 in particular mandates that the flag inventory "gains the same kind of equality test" as §8.2's, i.e. a deliberately matched pair of near-identical test bodies, which is what `dupl` is built to flag — while Non-Goal 7 forbids designing an abstraction to hold the merged form. The spec neither orders §6.1 against §7/§8 nor states that later tasks carry the same merge-or-exempt obligation, so a decomposer can produce a task set whose later closes go red for a reason §6.1 already anticipated and permitted.
suggestion: Add one sentence to §6.1: once enabled, `dupl` applies to every subsequent task in this release, and a clone introduced by a later task takes the same merge-or-exempt-with-recorded-reason decision at its own site. If §6.1 is meant to run late instead, state the ordering.

finding: §6.1 enables `dupl` "over production and test files alike, at its own default threshold" while Non-Goal 7 forbids merging any clone that would need a new abstraction. In a repo of 1099 test functions, table-driven setup blocks are the dominant clone form and their merge is precisely the abstraction Non-Goal 7 excludes — so the predicted outcome for the test-file half is not merges but per-site exemptions, each carrying "its reason recorded at the site". Every such exemption is a permanent line that every future reader (and every audit lens) parses, added by the section of a subtraction release; §2.3 then records a source-line count that this section pushes the wrong way. The spec never states what the instrument buys in return for that annotation burden.
suggestion: Either scope `dupl` to production files for this release (and name test-file duplication as a later version's problem), or state the budget that makes adoption honest: e.g. if a clone's only available disposition is exemption, the exemption is not written and the file is excluded — the linter is adopted for the clones it can actually retire. A one-line statement of "what we keep if merges are forbidden" is enough.

finding: §6.2 and §6.3 are the only sweeps with neither a tool nor a list to define their scope. §6.1 gets `dupl`'s output, §7.1 gets a committed enumeration produced by the release's first task, §8.2 and §8.3 get equality tests — but the set of one-call-site helpers, single-implementation interfaces, constant parameters and unreachable branches is never enumerated and no instrument is named to discover it. "Each is inlined" and "are removed rather than tested" therefore have no falsifiable completion: a task closing with two inlines and a task closing with twenty both conform, and a later reader cannot tell whether a surviving helper was judged to have a second caller or was never looked at.
suggestion: Name the discovery instrument for each (e.g. the sweep task's first output is the enumeration, in the shape §7.1 already uses), or state explicitly that §6.2 and §6.3 are opportunistic within the files the other tasks touch and make no completeness claim — so nobody audits them for one.

finding: The cap sentence "The sweep is capped at that list plus any test a removal decision depends on" sits inside §7.1, but §7's intro speaks of one sweep ("That is the instrument this sweep uses"), so it is unresolvable whether the cap binds only §7.1's mutation pass or all of §7. Both readings break something. If it binds only §7.1, then §7.2 (redundant assertions) and §7.3 (implementation-detail assertions) are uncapped over the 1099 test functions §7.1 just argued cannot be a scope, and a decomposer cannot size the task set. If it binds all of §7, then §7.2 is silently restricted to the v0.32.0→v0.33.0 window, which contradicts §7.2's own premise that the duplication accumulated because "each round of a past audit added one" — v0.32.0's 11-round audit and every earlier cycle sit outside that window.
suggestion: State the cap once, at §7 level, and say explicitly whether §7.2/§7.3 share the guard-test list as their scope. If §7.2/§7.3 are meant to reach outside the window, give them their own bound (e.g. only tests touched by a §7.1 removal decision, or only files already opened by another task in this release).

finding: The recorded fix for underdetermined-scope-derivation (high) was "The derivation is now mechanical" — "every test function added or modified" between two tags. Round 4 then showed the accompanying count (100 across 18 files) was a mixture of two rules and it was rightly deleted. But round 5 deleted the rule along with the count: the text now says the list runs "over the test functions **touched** between the v0.32.0 and v0.33.0 tags" and that "the exact rule and the resulting count are that task's output". "Touched" is strictly vaguer than "added or modified" (does a whitespace-only hunk, a rename, or a move count?), and with the rule itself delegated, no later round can check the first task's file against anything — the list becomes self-certifying, which matters because §7.1 makes it the cap on the entire sweep. The same edit also deleted the sentence warning that the derivation must pass `--no-ext-diff` because this repository configures an external diff driver whose output is not a unified diff. That was not merely decorative: without the flag the obvious command yields an empty result, so the failure mode this deletion re-enables is a first task that produces an empty or near-empty guard-test file and still closes as a completed deliverable.
suggestion: Keep the delegation of the count, but restore the two things that make the output auditable: a rule stated precisely enough to re-derive (added-or-modified, and what happens to renames), and the --no-ext-diff caveat, which is a property of this repository rather than a detail only code can settle.

finding: §7.1 gives the sweep an upper bound and no lower bound: "The sweep is capped at that list plus any test a removal decision depends on." Every other sentence describes what happens to a test once it is mutated, never that any given entry must be. A task that mutates five of the roughly hundred functions and reports them satisfies §7.1 word for word, and so does one that mutates all of them — no reviewer can tell an incomplete sweep from a complete one, and the file itself is only required to hold the list, not each entry's disposition. §6.1 has exactly the opposite property: the linter recomputes the outstanding set on every run, so completeness there is mechanical.
suggestion: State the per-entry obligation: every line in `spec/0.34.0-guard-tests.md` ends the release with a recorded disposition — mutation observed and kept, rewritten, or removed with surviving coverage named — so the file is the completion check. If a full pass is not intended, say which subset is in scope and drop the completeness implication.

finding: §8.1 states one placement rule — the canonical home is "the document the actor performing that task already has loaded" — and explicitly rejects topic as the criterion ("Ownership assigned by topic alone would move a fact an agent needs mid-cycle out of SKILL.md"). But the table marks both `skills/tp/SKILL.md` and `CLAUDE.md` as loaded by an agent every cycle, so the stated rule cannot discriminate between them; and the pair that overlaps most is exactly that one, since CLAUDE.md's self-development loop today holds decomposition rules and close recipes that the table assigns to SKILL.md. The section then resolves that pair by a second, unannounced criterion — "rules that are not about this repository at all" move to SKILL.md — which is topic, the criterion the section argued against.
suggestion: Name the tie-break for two documents that are both loaded: e.g. "when both are loaded, the narrower audience owns it — repo-specific facts stay in CLAUDE.md, facts true for every tp user move to SKILL.md" — and say that this is a scope rule rather than a topic rule, so it does not reopen the argument §8.1 already settled.

finding: §8.2 requires a test that fails "when the documented set and the emitted set diverge" for "every rule tp can emit", and correctly notes rules come from more than one package — but the harder boundary is not the package, it is the command. `Rule:` literals live in eight non-test files (cli/lint.go, engine/{entry,frontmatter,linecoverage,lint_rules,structured,vague,validate}.go) and the same struct field carries `tp validate` findings as well as `tp lint` findings, with four names (atomicity, coverage, line-coverage, schema) emitted by both. An honestly-collected "rules tp can emit" set therefore includes validate-only rules such as duplicate-id, self-dependency and unknown-dependency, which a README *lint* rule table should not list. Decomposition can source the sets, but not decide which command the table owns.
suggestion: Name the table's scope explicitly (the rules `tp lint` can emit) and say that the collected side must be restricted to the same command, since the emitting code does not distinguish lint findings from validate findings.

finding: The recorded fix (undefined-oracle and undefined-set-boundary, both medium) was "Section 8.3 states both sets: every flag registered on any command with persistent flags counted once, against the inventory in skills/tp/SKILL.md." Round 5 deleted the CLI-side rule outright. Persistent flags are the whole ambiguity it settled — tp registers --file, --json, --compact, --quiet and --no-color on root, so "a flag the CLI registers" is either five entries or five times the command count, and the section no longer says which. The documented side survives only by accident, in §8.1's unchanged closing sentence ("The checked inventory of §8.3 lives in SKILL.md"), not in §8.3 itself. Separately, the rewrite changed the test's shape while claiming it did not: it calls the check "the same kind of equality test" and then states one direction only — "it fails when a flag the CLI registers is undocumented". A documented flag that the CLI no longer registers passes, so the doc-side drift that §8 exists to remove is outside the check.
suggestion: Restore the CLI-side counting rule (one entry per flag, persistent flags counted once at the command that declares them) and state the check as a set equality in both directions, or stop calling it an equality and say explicitly that only undocumented-flag drift is caught.

finding: §9.2 says TestFileErrorsCarryAHint "is extended to enumerate ExitValidation sites the same way", and "the same way" is a single file-level exemption map (taskFileCommands) shared with the ExitFile walk. That map excuses set_local.go, set_project.go, config.go and config_extract.go as "task-file command"/"task-file/project config" — but their ExitValidation errors are about .tp/local.json and .tp/config.json, not the task file. Those nine sites (set_project.go x6, set_local.go x3) emit the code-1 default hint "run 'tp validate' to audit the task file" today, which is precisely the wrong-object defect §9.2 exists to remove; reusing the ExitFile exemption set would certify them as correct and let new ones join silently, contradicting the stated outcome ("a new site cannot join the class silently").
suggestion: State that the ExitValidation exemption set is derived independently of the ExitFile one — a file may be excused for the code-3 default and still owe a hint for the code-1 default — and name the config/local commands as in scope for the fix, not as exemptions.

finding: Round 5 moved the model-comparison recipe from skills/tp/SKILL.md to "the reference", citing §8.1's placement rule. §8.1 is unchanged, and its ownership table gives the Reference row "Exhaustive field, exit-code and schema detail" — an operator procedure for comparing two models across review rounds is none of those three. §10.2 satisfies the table's "Loaded by" column (Either, on demand) while falling outside every Owns row, so under §8.1's own instruction that "anything duplicated across two homes is cut from the non-owner" the recipe has no owner to be cut back to. The earlier recorded fix here (unnamed-canonical-home, low) was satisfied by naming a home; the new home is named but is one whose stated scope excludes the content. Note also that the file is skills/tp/REFERENCE.md, inside the skill directory, which blurs the human-versus-agent split the table is built on.
suggestion: Either widen §8.1's Reference row to cover on-demand operator procedures as well as field and schema detail, or name a different home for the recipe. A one-line edit to the Owns column is enough.

finding: §10.2 places the model-diversity recipe in "the reference" and cites §8.1's placement rule as the justification. But §8.1's table gives that document a narrow ownership — "Exhaustive field, exit-code and schema detail" — which a procedural recipe is not, so the placement satisfies the loaded-by column while contradicting the owns column of the same row. The row is also the only one in the table that names no file (the other three are backticked paths), so §10.2 mandates writing into a document the spec never identifies.
suggestion: Either widen the Reference row's Owns cell to cover operator-facing procedures and on-demand recipes, or give §10.2 a different home; in both cases name the reference document by path in the §8.1 table so the task has a target file.

finding: The section written this round to replace the deleted test list opens with a measured claim about the review record that does not reproduce: "Four review rounds produced eleven blocking findings that were all instances of one shape: the list and its section drifted." Counted over spec/.tp-review/0.34.0/review-round-1..4.ndjson, findings located at §12 number 32 in total, of which 17 are blocking (critical or high) — 3, 5, 4 and 5 across the four rounds. They are also not one shape: they span non-discriminating test recipes (the interleaving that could not fail), unbuildable oracles (the mutation record, the frozen guard-marker set), assertions contradicting an existing contract (import does not merge), and a coverage gap (no item distinguished a lock taken before the read from one taken after). This is the class round 4 recorded high against §7.1 (measured-claim-not-reproducible), whose fix was to delete an unreproducible count — reintroduced in the very section written to carry that repair. It is not load-bearing for any task, but it is a checkable claim about the record in a release whose thesis is that recorded state should be true.
suggestion: Drop the numbers and the single-shape characterisation, or state them as counted: seventeen blocking findings across four rounds, in several shapes, all traceable to the list restating its section. The argument for deleting the list does not need the number to be small.

finding: §12's opening paragraph spends four lines narrating this spec's own review history ("Earlier drafts carried a numbered test list here ... Four review rounds produced eleven blocking findings that were all instances of one shape ..."). The instruction inside it — do not re-add the list, each section states its own outcome — feeds a real decomposition decision; the round count and finding count feed none, and they are read by every downstream consumer of this spec (decomposer, spec-coverage checklist, future readers) forever. The same shape appears in §5 ("four routes have already been proposed in review and three of them were disproven by measurement") and §7.1 ("three of the guards written during it were found not to guard"), though in those two the history is load-bearing: it tells the reader why prose cannot close the question, which prevents a round trip. In §12 it does not.
suggestion: Keep the operative sentence ("Each section above states the outcome that must become observably true; the assertion is authored as task acceptance") and the `over-specification` framing, and cut the round/finding accounting — the review record already lives in `spec/.tp-review/`, which is the canonical home for it under §8.1.

finding: §5 leaves "which override to remove, by what route" to decomposition, but every route to removing a task-level `quality_gate` sits outside the ordinary agent path: `quality_gate` is init-authored and read-only at the task level (`tp set --workflow` rejects it), and hand-editing `<base>.tasks.json` is fenced off from the implementing unit. The section does not acknowledge that the surviving routes may require an operator action or a re-init rather than a task step, so a decomposer can author a task whose acceptance no permitted action can reach.
suggestion: Add one sentence naming the constraint rather than the route: the override cannot be edited by `tp set` and the task file cannot be hand-edited by the implementing unit, so whatever route decomposition settles on must be expressible as a supported command or be recorded as an operator step.

finding: §6.1 scopes merge-or-exempt to the enabling task ("Every clone it reports is either merged or exempted"), but .golangci.yml runs at every close for the rest of the release. Measured on today's tree, dupl at its default threshold reports 13 issues (6 clone pairs), several between near-identical test functions only ~16 lines long (internal/engine/configresolve_test.go:153 vs :185). §8.2 and §8.3 then mandate two equality tests explicitly described as "the same kind" — exactly that clone shape — so a later task can close red on a duplication the spec itself ordered, and Non-Goal 7 forbids factoring them into a shared helper.
suggestion: State that the merge-or-exempt rule (and the Non-Goal 7 exemption) governs every task after the enabling one, not just that task, so a mandated twin test is exempted at the site rather than blocking the close.

finding: §7.1 creates `spec/0.34.0-guard-tests.md`, a committed file of the order of a hundred `file:function` lines, and never says who reads it after the sweep closes. It is a work queue, not a fact: once the sweep is done, every line is either a test that was kept or a test that no longer exists. §8.1's table has no owner row that fits it and §2.1 requires a documentation removal to name the one place the fact now lives — so this release adds a permanent document that its own contracts have no rule for, in the release whose governing rule is subtraction.
suggestion: State the file's lifecycle in one sentence: either it is deleted (or truncated to its outcome — counts and dispositions) by the last sweep task, or it is named as a durable record with the reader who consults it. Naming it a working artifact costs one line and removes a permanent one.

finding: §7.1 says "The exact rule and the resulting count are that task's output" and, in the same paragraph, "it is of the order of a hundred functions". The second sentence is load-bearing — it is the stated reason triage ordering belongs to that task — but it is not stated as binding or non-binding. If the derivation yields thirty or four hundred, one engineer treats the estimate as a sanity bound and reworks the rule until it lands near a hundred, another records the count and moves on. That is the same first task producing two different lists, which is the outcome the fixed-list mechanism exists to prevent.
suggestion: Mark it non-binding in the text — whatever the stated rule yields is the list, the estimate only explains why triage ordering is anticipated — or drop the figure and keep the triage requirement unconditional.
